full_judgment:
"Let a Rule be issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why the impugned order No. 17 dated 20-1-2016 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 630 of 2014 appointing the sole arbitrator should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper." 

 2. Facts leading to the issue of the Rule is that the opposite party filed a miscellaneous proceeding under the provision of the Arbitration Act, 2001 before the competent court being Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 630 of 2014 impleading the petitioner as opposite parties for appointment of arbitrator as per the section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. The court below proceeded with the proceeding and by the impugned judgment and order appointed an arbitrator by following the provisions of law. 

 5. Mr Sameer Sattar, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submits that the court below in the present case in hand committed an error in appointing an arbitrator as there is no arbitration clause as per the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 2001. He submits that in the absence of a valid arbitration agreement the opposite party cannot pray for an appointment of arbitrator under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. He submits that the alleged arbitration clause is not an arbitration agreement and, as such, the court below committed an error in passing the impugned judgment and order. By referring the provisions of section 9 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 he submits that an arbitration agreement may be in the form of an arbitration clause in a contract or in the Form of a separate agreement. He submits that the arbitration clause as alleged does not cover the ingredients of section 9 of the Arbitration Act, 2001. He further submits that though the petitioner has challenged the impugned order, but since the question of law has been raised this court has the jurisdiction to see the legality and propriety of the entire proceeding. He submits that admittedly the petitioner is a bank incorporated under the provision of the Banking Companies Act and for the purpose of loan recovery there is a special law, namely Artha Rin Adalat Ain which contained several non-obstantive clause as much as it is now well settled a proposition of law is that in a loan recovery case relates to a schedule bank there is no other option but to invoke the jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 as amended. By referring several provisions of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 2003 he submits that if there is a conflict in between the Arbitration Act and the Artha Rin Adalat Ain shall prevail. By referring the provisions of section 5(1) read with section 3 of the Act of 2003. He submits that there is a clear non-obstantive clause specify the realization of loan process granted by a bank as per section 5 of the Act of 2003 an exclusive jurisdiction has been vested upon the Artha Rin Adalat. By referring the section 20 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain he further submits that a competent suit is being pending before a competent Artha Rin Adalat Ain and as per the provisions of law the proceeding cannot be challenged in any other proceeding. 

 6. Mr NAM Razzaque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party vehemently opposes the Rule. By referring the counter-affidavit he submits that the court below in the present case in hand committed no error in allowing an arbitration miscellaneous proceeding as much as appointment of an arbitrator because of a specific arbitration agreement in between the parties. He submits that by inserting specific arbitration clause the petitioner bank submitted itself into this jurisdiction of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and, as such, any other proceeding over lacking the arbitration proceeding is not maintainable in the eye of law. He submits that arbitration proceeding being a special law is superior than any other law for the time being and referred the decisions reported in 65 DLR (AD) 4. He further submits that by giving consent regarding the appointment of arbitrator the petitioner waived his right and thereby governed by the principle of waiver and cannot challenge the same in a later stage. In support of his contention the leaned Advocate referred the decision reported in 61 DLR 628. 

 10. In the present case in hand it appears that the bank who is the petitioner initiated a legal proceeding by filing of Artha Rin Suit before the competent Artha Rin Adalat as per section 5 of the Act of 2003. After filing of the Artha Rin Suit the opposite party invoked the provision of the Arbitration Act, 2001 by way of filing miscellaneous proceeding for an appointment of arbitrator under the provisions of the Arbitration Act, 2001. It is apparent that initially the petitioner consented the proceeding but ultimately challenged the impugned judgment and order. 

 14. In the present case in hand it is to be noted that in the said dispute clause it has been mentioned that in the event of any dispute between the parties they shall try to resolve the dispute amicably only. There is nothing mentioned about the invocation of the arbitration proceeding in any manner. In the second part of dispute clause it has been mentioned that in the event of failure to resolve it shall be referred to the competent court in Bangladesh and the dispute shall be governed by and construed in accordance with law of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. 

 16. So, it appears that though section 7 as well as section 10 relates to the provisions which discouraged the invocation of any other jurisdiction if there is a specific arbitration clause. But at the same time, section 3 sub-section (3) of the Act of 2001 categorically stated that this act shall not affect any other law for the time being in force by virtue of which certain dispute may not be submitted to arbitration. It is to be noted that to invoke the provision of the arbitration as per the provision of Act 1 of 2001 there must be an arbitration agreement as per section 9 of the Act. In the present case in hand it is very much clear that in the dispute clause it has been only mentioned that the parties shall try to resolve the dispute amicably. 

 23. So it appears that unlike any other laws an inherent power has been vested in the Act of 2003 which clearly show's that the law itself is a special in nature. Since in the present case in hand though the petitioner has challenged the impugned order but a serious question has been raised and, as such, we are of the view that exercising the power conferred under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 this court can see the legality and propriety of the entire proceeding itself. We have no disagreement with the decision of their lordships regarding the nature of Act of 2001 but the facts and circumstances are quite different and the decision as reported in 61 DLR 628 is not applicable because there is a question of law involved. The principle of waiver cannot give aid to any proceeding which is beyond jurisdiction or suffers from legal infirmity.
